hook: The envoy who walked into the unknown west and opened the way for the Silk Road.

pages.x: In 138 BC Emperor Wu of Han wanted allies against the Xiongnu, the nomad horsemen who raided China. He sent a palace officer, Zhang Qian, west with about 100 men to find the Yuezhi, a people the Xiongnu had driven far away.

Almost at once the Xiongnu caught him. He was held for ten years, married a Xiongnu wife and had a son, but kept the staff that marked him as the emperor's envoy. Then he escaped, and instead of going home, carried on west.

He crossed the Pamir mountains into Central Asia, to Ferghana, Sogdiana and Bactria, lands no Chinese had seen. The Yuezhi did not want war, but he came back with news of rich cities, of Persia and India, and of the "heavenly horses" of Ferghana, said to sweat blood.

Captured again on the way back, he escaped once more and reached the capital in 125 BC, thirteen years after he had left. Of the hundred men who set out, only he and one other came home. The emperor made him a lord.
pages.cap: A wall painting at Dunhuang shows him setting out

pages.x: His reports opened China's eyes to the west. Han armies and merchants followed his route: Chinese silk went west, while horses, grapes and alfalfa, and later Buddhism, came east. He is often called the father of the Silk Road.
Zhang Qian was the first official traveller to link China with Central Asia. The trade routes that followed him carried goods, ideas and religions between East and West for 1,500 years.
pts: Explored Central Asia for the Han emperor
Survived ten years as a prisoner
Opened the way for the Silk Road
